name: Daria Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shift lead at a big commercial bakery, the kind that makes the sliced bread and the cheap croissants you see in every supermarket. I look after the tunnel oven, which is forty metres long, and the slicing and bagging lines after it. My job is keeping the bake even, sorting out whatever breaks, and making sure my team of seven gets their breaks and doesn't get burned. I like the smell, people think you'd get sick of it, but I never have.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a hard day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A hard day is when the dough comes through wrong from the mixing room, too wet, and everything downstream goes to pieces. Loaves stick in the slicer, the bagger jams, and I've got pallets waiting. My partner Luis is an electrician and he says I come home talking about dough like it's a person who let me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, it's a useful tool and nothing more. I use a chatbot now and then for writing staff rotas and the odd awkward email, and it's handy for that. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not big online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, and that's mostly fine by me. Luis and I bought a small house last year, we've got savings and decent jobs, and the bakery isn't going anywhere because people always need bread. I'd keep my head down and keep doing a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage a little each month like we do now and keep our savings where they are. Maybe I'd use the AI tools a bit more for paperwork if the bakery brought something in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like hearing the forecast is the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your job where you'd welcome a bit more help from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the planning. Every Thursday I spend two hours juggling who's off, who's on holiday, who can't do nights because of their kids. If a computer could do my rota, I'd buy it a cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what part would you never hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Judging the bake. I look at the crust colour coming out of the oven and I know if the third zone is running hot. Maybe a camera could do it, but I've been right about that oven more times than the sensor has.

S0.say: I'd say fine, it's a useful tool and nothing more. I use a chatbot now and then for rotas and awkward emails, but I wouldn't post anything about it.
S0.think: Privately things stay as they are, and that mostly suits me. Luis and I have a new house, savings and decent jobs, and people always need bread.
S0.do: Keeps overpaying the mortgage a little each month and leaves savings as they are. Uses AI tools a bit more for paperwork if the bakery brings something in.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast that matches yesterday.
S0.quote: If a computer could do my rota, I'd buy it a cake.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is settled and practical, with a new house and a partner in a different trade. She treats AI as a helper for dull admin like rotas. Her pride is in reading the oven by eye, and she quietly trusts herself over the sensors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be sensible and train people up rather than panic. If someone at work asked, I'd tell them to learn whatever new machines come in. I'd be careful not to sound like I'm on management's side or the union's, I'd just say be practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think bagging and packing go first, because big bakeries elsewhere already use robots on those lines. The oven might stay with people longer. My job might change from fixing things to watching screens, and I'd have to get used to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the bakery actually buys, and when it did, I'd ask to be on the first group trained on it. I'd use the AI tools more once a couple of the other leads said they were worth it. We'd keep saving and keep the mortgage overpayments going, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly for the packing team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the packing team.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Aisha and Grace and a few agency workers who come and go. Aisha's been there twelve years and she can pack faster than the machine on a bad day. The machine doesn't get tired at four in the morning, and Aisha does, and that's the whole argument right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs to stay ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. There are plenty of other food factories around here, but they'd be doing the same thing. I'd rather be the one at this bakery who knows the new kit than start over somewhere else.

S1.say: I'd say it's happening, so let's train people rather than panic. I'd tell colleagues to learn whatever comes in and keep to being practical rather than taking sides.
S1.think: Privately bagging and packing would go first, while the oven stays with people longer. My job might shift from fixing things to watching screens.
S1.do: Waits to see what the bakery buys, then asks to be in the first group trained on it. Uses AI tools more once other leads vouch for them and keeps saving and overpaying the mortgage.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, mostly on behalf of the packing team.
S1.quote: The machine doesn't get tired at four in the morning, and Aisha does, and that's the whole argument right there.
S1.fieldNote: Daria waits for proof and then moves to the front of the queue for training. She stays carefully neutral between management and union. Her concern is for packers like Aisha, and she put the economics of tiredness very plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should have been ready for this. I'd want help for people who lose work, but I'd also say people need to get on with it. I wouldn't be shouting, I'd just be talking to people at work and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the bakery would close or go almost fully automatic in that time. Luis would probably last longer, because robots doing wiring in old houses sounds harder than robots bagging bread. So we'd probably have one wage for a while, and I'd hate that, but we'd survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and keep the cash in the bank instead, so we'd have more to hand. We'd cut the holiday and eating out. I'd ask Luis about helping on his jobs, carrying and pulling cable to start with, and see if I could start an electrical apprenticeship. And we'd put off having kids, which we'd been talking about for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Worried, but not lost, because of Luis and the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off kids is a big step. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. Luis's mum asks about grandchildren every Sunday. I'd tell her we're waiting to see if the robots leave us a wage first, and she'd think I was joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Luis would last longer. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, if I'm honest. Two years is fast and the card said hands-on work too. I'm hoping, more than I'm sure.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and the government should have been ready. I'd want help for people who lose work, but also say people need to get on with it.
S2.think: Privately the bakery would close or go almost fully automatic, while Luis's wiring work might last longer. We'd likely live on one wage for a while and survive.
S2.do: Stops the extra mortgage payments to keep more cash on hand and cuts holidays and eating out. Starts helping Luis on his jobs with an eye to an electrical apprenticeship and puts off having children, planned for next year.
S2.feel: Anxious but not lost, thanks to Luis's income and their savings.
S2.quote: I'd tell her we're waiting to see if the robots leave us a wage first, and she'd think I was joking.
S2.fieldNote: Daria's calm rests largely on Luis's trade lasting longer than hers, and she admits that is a hope rather than a certainty. Delaying children is the biggest personal cost she names. She stays pragmatic, wanting both government help and personal effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to plan if they're told the truth early. I'd tell people at work to start learning something now and not to wait for a letter. I'd want the government and employers to put money into courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is enough for me to switch to Luis's trade, or something next to it. I'd be qualified by 30. Whether electricians are safe by 2031 is another question, but it's a better bet than packing bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time electrical course in the first year and work weekends with Luis. I'd stay on at the bakery for the wage until I was qualified. We'd keep overpaying the mortgage, so that by 2031 there's less owed, and maybe we'd still try for a baby after year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, so it's less scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it be, working for your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a few arguments about how to coil a cable. He's very fussy. We've shared a kitchen for three years, so I think we could share a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If electricians aren't safe either, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least we'd own more of the house and have some money put aside. I don't know what comes after that, nobody does. I'd rather be ready for most of it than worry about all of it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people are told the truth early. I'd tell colleagues to start learning now and want government and employers funding courses.
S3.think: Privately five years is enough to switch to Luis's trade and be qualified by 30. It may not be safe either, but it's a better bet than packing bread.
S3.do: Starts a part-time electrical course in year one, works weekends with Luis and stays at the bakery for the wage until qualified. Keeps overpaying the mortgage and may still try for a baby after year two.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with the plan making it less scary.
S3.quote: We've shared a kitchen for three years, so I think we could share a van.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Daria has a clear plan: retrain into her partner's trade while keeping her wage. She accepts that even electricians may not be safe and settles for being mostly ready. Her humour about sharing a van shows a steady, grounded relationship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd want schools and colleges to change what they teach. I'd probably say that to anyone who'd listen, but quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think ten years is long enough to have a normal life and still change. We'd have kids, I'd keep my job for a good while, and I'd switch trades halfway. I'd be 37 by then, plenty young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years, I'd keep working at the bakery and get trained on whatever new kit came in. Around year four, I'd start the electrical course with Luis. We'd go ahead with having a baby next year as planned and keep paying down the mortgage, so by 2036 it's mostly ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels far enough off that we can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say ten years makes people complacent. Would that be you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. But I've got a plan with dates on it. I'd write it on the calendar in the kitchen, next to the bin days, so I can't pretend I forgot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do something with people, and learn to use whatever the machines are. That's about all I'd know. And maybe learn to bake, because it's nice even if a robot can do it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd want schools and colleges to change what they teach.
S4.think: Privately ten years is long enough for a normal life and still a change of trade. We'd have kids, I'd keep my job a while and switch halfway, at 37 still young enough.
S4.do: Keeps working at the bakery and trains on new kit for the first few years, then starts the electrical course with Luis around year four. Goes ahead with having a baby next year and keeps paying down the mortgage.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with the change far enough off to plan around.
S4.quote: I'd write it on the calendar in the kitchen, next to the bin days, so I can't pretend I forgot.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Daria keep her family plans and still switch trades on a timetable. She guards against complacency by writing the plan on the kitchen calendar. Her advice to a future child mixes people skills, technology and baking for its own sake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the one where we'd have to put our lives on hold, the baby, the house, all of it. Two years isn't enough time to learn a new trade, it's barely enough time to finish a mortgage form. What would help is paid courses you could start straight away, and some kind of guarantee for people with mortgages so they don't lose their homes while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the bread. If robots make everything, will it still taste the same? I'd like to think someone still cares if the crust is right.

headlineQuote: Two years isn't enough time to learn a new trade, it's barely enough time to finish a mortgage form.
portrait: Daria Garcia, 27, is a shift lead on a tunnel oven and bagging lines at a large commercial bakery, practical and quietly proud of reading the bake by eye. She and her partner Luis, an electrician, bought a small house last year and plan to have a child. She waits for proof before taking up new tools but then asks to be first in line for training. A plateau and steady disruption leave her calm to uneasy, while fast AGI makes her anxious and leads her to delay children and start learning Luis's trade. With five or ten years she builds a dated plan to switch trades while keeping her family plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would force her and Luis to put their lives, including having a baby, on hold.
whatWouldHelp: Paid courses she could start straight away and some guarantee that people with mortgages won't lose their homes while they retrain.
